messages.subject: Allometric effects
parts:
I am checking for differences in skull shape in two species. Even though these species are similar in size I want to avoid allometric effects, so I am using the code below:

# identifiers
species<-c("A", "B", "B", "B", "A"...
individuals<-c("CPI10589", "CPI10590"...

landmark_list<-list(CPI10589_OnMK_skull_1, CPI10590_OnFK_skull_1...
data_array <- abind::abind(landmark_list, along = 3,new.names=ind)

# GPA
gpa_result <- gpagen(data_array,
                     curves=curves,
                     ProcD=FALSE, print.progress = TRUE)

#extracting symmetric component
symmetry_result <- bilat.symmetry(
  A = data_array,
  ind = individuals,  # Individual identifier, if needed
  object.sym = TRUE,  # TRUE for object symmetry, FALSE for matching symmetry
  land.pairs = sym_pairs,  # Pairs of symmetric landmarks
  curve = curves,  # Curve data for sliding landmarks
  iter = 1000,  # Number of iterations for randomization tests
  seed = NULL  # Seed for reproducibility
)
symmetry <- symmetry_result$symm.shape

#allometry
size<-gpa_result$Csize
allometry_sp<-procD.lm(symmetry~species,iter=999)
allometry_sp_resid<-allometry_sp$residuals #extracting residuals from the regression

######### my doubts are in the following steps ###########

1. Since I want to avoid allometric effects, I should run the PCA with the residuals obtained from my regression (allometry_sp_resid), correct?

#PCA
pca_result_resid <- gm.prcomp(allometry_sp_resid)
pc_scores_resid <- pca_result_resid$x
pc_data_resid <- data.frame(PC1 = pc_scores_resid[, 1],
                      PC2 = pc_scores_resid[, 2],
                      PC3 = pc_scores_resid[, 3],
                      Individual = individuals,
                      species = species)

#Visualization
skull2308<-file2mesh("PK2308_OnFY_skull_1.stl" , clean = TRUE, readcol = FALSE)
ref<-mshape(symmetry) #symmetric component aligned data object
refmesh <- warpRefMesh(skull2308,symmetry[,,7], ref, color=NULL, centered=T)
mesh2obj(refmesh, filename = refmesh, writeNormals = TRUE)
refmeshstl<-file2mesh("refmesh.stl" , clean = TRUE, readcol = FALSE)

2. Here is my second doubt. I am trying to plot my shape predictions using:

sc.preds_1_resid <- shape.predictor(symmetry, x= PC1_resid, Intercept = FALSE,pred1 = min(PC1_resid), pred2 = max(PC1_resid))
plotPC1min_vec<-plotRefToTarget(ref, sc.preds_1_resid$pred1, method = "vector",mag = 1,gridPars = GP)

Should I use A="symmetry" or allometry_sp$GM$fitted?

Thanks again,

Bruno

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Allometric effects
parts:
Bruno,

Before discussing how to “avoid allometric effects”, it might be wise to question whether allometric effects should be avoided. When one tries to remove an allometric effect, they are removing a common allometric effect, because there is no removing of unique allometries for comparison of means. If the allometries are in any way unique, then seeking to compare means would be foolhardy. Assuming you have confirmed that all group allometries are parallel,

1. I would perform PCA or other subsequent analyses on residuals from allometry added to the overall shape mean (again, only after confirming allometries are not unique). The purpose of this answers question #2. 

2. You need to maintain the mean configuration along with the residuals for shape.predictor, otherwise a deformation of the mean shape would not make sense with data that do not contain the mean shape. So add the mean shape to all residuals. Which scores to use for prediction depends on purpose. Showing how shape changes along PC 1 or PC 1 of fitted values are different things. Showing how shape changes at each LS mean is another different thing.  Showing how shape changes at minimum and maximum sizes, or any sizes, for unique allometries is yet another different thing. Define the purpose and predict shapes accordingly.  Your question for which set of data to use for visualization does not state a clear visualization purpose, so a recommendation is difficult. 

Good luck!

Mike

parts:
Dear Mike,

Thank you very much for your response and assistance! Reflecting on your advice, I explored shape changes between the sexes within each species by using a violin plot of size distribution and conducting a trajectory analysis (see the code below). It appears you were correct—working with residuals in this case may not be worthwhile, as the difference in trajectory lengths (0.0046) between the two species is small and not statistically significant (p = 0.35). 

#########################################################################
traj_model<-procD.lm(symmetry~species*sex)
Trajectory<-trajectory.analysis(traj_model,groups = species,traj.pts = sex)
sex_colors <- c("red","blue")
{TP<-plot(Trajectory,pch=as.numeric(as.factor(species))+20,bg=sex_colors[as.factor(sex)])
  add.trajectories(TP, traj.pch = c(21, 22),
                   start.bg = 1, end.bg = 1)
  legend("topright", levels(as.factor(species)), pch = c(21, 22))
  legend("bottomleft", levels(as.factor(sex)), pch = 19,
         col = c("red","blue"))}
########################################################################

Trajectory analysis

1000 permutations.

Points projected onto trajectory PCs

Trajectories:
Trajectories hidden (use show.trajectories = TRUE to view)

Observed path distances by group

    Onigra  Oquelchii 
0.02031957 0.02493608 

Pairwise absolute differences in path distances, plus statistics
                           d   UCL (95%)         Z Pr > d
Onigra:Oquelchii 0.004616508 0.009201343 0.4827864   0.35

Best regards,
